docs.title: NetBox Routing Protocols
docs.text:
A NetBox plugin to document the routing configuration of your network: static routes, BGP, OSPF, IS-IS and EIGRP, together with the objects they use (prefix lists, route maps, AS paths, communities) and BFD profiles.

NetBox already knows your devices, interfaces, IP addresses, prefixes, VRFs, ASNs and tenants. This plugin adds the routing layer on top of them, so the answer to "which routers speak OSPF in area 0.0.0.10?", "which peers use this prefix list?" or "what is the SRGB of this IS-IS instance?" is one search away, next to the rest of your inventory.

The plugin documents, it does not configure. The plugin stores the intended routing configuration. It never connects to a device. Use it as the source of truth that your templates, automation or documentation read from, through the NetBox UI, REST API or GraphQL.

docs.title: What is covered
docs.text: Area What you can describe Page Static routes Prefix, next hop, interface, VRF, metric, tag, the devices that carry the route Static routes BGP Routers, VRF scopes, address families, peers, session/peer/policy templates, settings BGP OSPF (v2, IPv4) Instances, areas, interfaces, networks, authentication, redistribution, virtual links, summaries, ranges, neighbors, traffic engineering, segment routing, fast reroute OSPF IS-IS Instances, interfaces, levels, authentication, segment routing, Flex-Algo, SRv6 IS-IS EIGRP Routers (classic and named), address families, networks, interfaces EIGRP Routing objects Prefix lists, route maps, AS paths, communities and community lists Routing objects BFD Reusable BFD timer profiles BFD

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
• Never used it? Read Using the plugin: the menu, how objects relate to each other, and what every list and form offers.
  • Looking for a feature? Each protocol page lists its features, fields and the RFC they come from. The RFC index goes the other way: from an RFC to the features that use it.
  • Installing? See the README.

docs.title: Why the RFCs are mentioned
docs.text: Routing protocols have precise rules: allowed ranges, default timers, which options require which. The plugin follows the standards, so the field names, defaults and validations match what the RFC says and what your routers implement. Wherever a feature or a default comes from an RFC, the page says which one and, when it is not obvious, why it is there. Vendor-specific features without an RFC are marked as such.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• NetBox 4.7 or newer.
  • PostgreSQL, as NetBox itself.

docs.title: BFD
docs.text:
Routing → BFD → BFD Profile

Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (RFC 5880) detects a failed link or neighbor in milliseconds, much faster than the routing protocols' own hello timers. A BFD profile is a named set of timers you define once and reuse, so every peer that should detect failures in the same time points at the same profile.

Field Meaning (RFC 5880 name) Name How the profile is referred to. Min TX interval The minimum interval the router wants to send BFD packets at (Desired Min TX Interval). Min RX interval The minimum interval it can receive them at (Required Min RX Interval). Multiplier How many consecutive packets may be lost before the session is declared down (Detect Mult). The detection time is the negotiated interval times this value. Hold Optional hold time, for platforms that have one. It is not part of the RFC. Tenant Optional owner.

Where it is used:

  • A BGP session template or a BGP peer can point at a BFD profile.
  • OSPF, IS-IS and EIGRP interfaces only have a BFD on/off switch; they do not use profiles, because the timers of those protocols come from the interface configuration of the device.

Note. The plugin does not check the intervals against what your platform supports. Choose values your hardware can sustain: a profile with very small intervals on a busy router causes false failures.

docs.title: Development
docs.text: For people who want to run the plugin from source or contribute.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/baldoarturo/netbox-routing-protocols
cd netbox-routing-protocols
dev/run.sh

dev/run.sh installs podman if needed, downloads NetBox, creates the virtual environment, starts PostgreSQL and Redis, loads the NetBox demo data and starts NetBox on http://localhost:8000 (user admin, password admin). It can be run again at any time. The full explanation, the options and how to run the tests are in dev/README.md.

docs.title: Work on these docs
docs.text:
The documentation is Markdown in docs/, built with MkDocs and the Material theme.

pip install -r docs/requirements.txt
mkdocs serve        # preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000, reloads on save
mkdocs build --strict

--strict fails on broken links, which is what the publishing workflow runs.

When you add or change a feature, update its section in the page of the protocol, with the RFC it comes from and why it exists when that is not obvious, and add the RFC to the RFC index.

docs.title: Publishing
docs.text: The site is published to GitHub Pages by the docs workflow when main changes. The repository needs Pages enabled with the source set to GitHub Actions and the repository variable DOCS_PAGES set to true; until then the workflow only checks that the site builds.

docs.title: Routing objects
docs.text:
Routing → Routing Objects

Routing objects are the building blocks that policies are made of. They are not tied to one protocol: today BGP policy templates and peer address families point at prefix lists and route maps.

About the standards. Prefix lists, route maps and AS-path filters are vendor features: no RFC defines them, and every vendor spells them a little differently. What the RFCs define is what they act on: IP prefixes (RFC 4632 for IPv4 CIDR, RFC 4291 for IPv6), the BGP AS_PATH attribute (RFC 4271 §5.1.2) and BGP communities (RFC 1997). Those are the pieces the plugin validates.

docs.title: Prefix lists
docs.text:
Prefix Lists and Prefix List Entries

A prefix list is an ordered list of rules; each rule says permit or deny the prefixes it matches. Routers evaluate the entries in sequence order and stop at the first that matches.

docs.title: Prefix list
docs.text: Field Meaning Name Name of the list, as used in the device configuration. Family IPv4 or IPv6. A list holds only one family, and the family cannot be changed once the list exists (its entries would stop making sense).

docs.title: Prefix list entry
docs.text:
Field Meaning Prefix list The list the entry belongs to. Sequence Evaluation order, 1 to 4294967294 (the range routers accept). Leave it empty and the form suggests the next free one; the API assigns it automatically. Action Permit or Deny. Prefix A prefix from NetBox IPAM (IPAM → Prefixes). It must be of the family of the list. Any Matches the all-zeros prefix of the family (0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0). NetBox IPAM cannot hold that prefix, so this checkbox stands for it. With LE set to the longest length (32 or 128) it matches every prefix. Leave Prefix empty when you use it. GE / LE The length range of the match, as on routers. GE ("greater than or equal") and LE ("less than or equal") are lengths, not counts.

How to read GE and LE for a prefix 10.0.0.0/8:

GE LE Matches – – exactly 10.0.0.0/8 16 – any prefix inside 10.0.0.0/8 of length 16 or longer, up to /32 – 24 10.0.0.0/8 and everything inside it up to /24 16 24 prefixes inside 10.0.0.0/8 with a length from 16 to 24

The plugin refuses a GE or LE that is shorter than the prefix, longer than the family allows (32 for IPv4, 128 for IPv6) or when GE is greater than LE.

A prefix used by a list is protected. A NetBox prefix referenced by a prefix list entry cannot be deleted, and a change to it that would make an entry invalid (for example shortening the prefix below the entry's GE) is refused, with a message that names the entries. Remove or edit the entries first.

docs.title: Overlap warnings
docs.text:
When you save an entry the plugin compares it with the other entries of the list and warns (it still saves) about:

Warning Meaning Duplicate Another entry matches exactly the same prefixes. Shadowed An earlier entry matches everything this one matches, so this entry is never reached. Shadows This entry matches everything a later entry matches, so that later entry is never reached. Nested One covers the other, with the more specific first. This is the normal way to write an exception, so it is shown for information. Overlaps They share some prefixes but neither covers the other.

The entry's detail page lists the overlapping entries, and a prefix list's page shows where the list is used.

docs.title: Search Prefix Match
docs.text:
Routing → Routing Objects → Search Prefix Match

Type a prefix or a plain address (10.0.0.0/24, 192.0.2.1, 2001:db8::/32) and the page shows, as you type, which prefix list entries match it, in which sequence, and whether the entry permits or denies it. An address is treated as a host prefix. Tick Include the lists with no match to see the lists that do not match too. It answers "would this prefix get through that filter?" without logging in to a router. It needs the view permission on prefix list entries.

docs.title: Route maps
docs.text:
Route Maps and Route Map Entries

A route map is an ordered list of rules like a prefix list, but each rule can match several attributes and set others.

Field Meaning Route map Name of the map. Sequence Evaluation order. Action Permit or Deny. Flow control (continue) Sequence to continue evaluating at after this entry matches, for platforms that support continue. Match prefix list / community list / community / AS path Link the entry to the NetBox objects it matches on. Match parameters / Set parameters Free-form JSON for everything the links do not cover (for example a local preference to set). The plugin stores it as written; it does not interpret it.

docs.title: AS paths
docs.text:
AS Path and AS Path Entries

An AS-path list filters routes by the sequence of autonomous systems they crossed (the BGP AS_PATH attribute, RFC 4271 §5.1.2). Each entry has a sequence, an action (permit or deny) and a pattern: a regular expression in the syntax of your platform. The pattern is not validated, because every vendor's regex dialect differs.

docs.title: Communities
docs.text:
Community List, Community and Community List Entry

BGP communities (RFC 1997) are 32-bit tags attached to routes so that policies can act on groups of routes. By convention they are written ASN:value, for example 65000:100. Keep the list of the communities you use as Community objects, so the meaning of 65000:100 is documented once:

Field Meaning Community The community value, for example 65000:100. Name Optional human name ("customer routes"). Status Active, Reserved or Deprecated, to retire a community without deleting its history. Role A NetBox IPAM role that classifies the community (for example blackhole, customer). Tenant Optional owner.

A Community List groups communities under a name, and its entries each have an action (permit or deny) and a community, evaluated like a prefix list. Route map entries can match on a community or on a whole community list.

docs.title: The menu
docs.text:
Everything lives under Routing in the NetBox navigation menu, grouped like this:

Group Entries Routing Objects Community List, Community, Community List Entry, Prefix Lists, Prefix List Entries, Search Prefix Match, Route Maps, Route Map Entries, AS Path, AS Path Entries BFD BFD Profile Static Static Routes BGP Settings, Peer Templates, Policy Templates, Session Templates, Routers, Scopes, Address Families, Peers, Peer Address Families OSPF Instances, Areas, Interfaces, Networks, Redistribution, Virtual Links, Summary Addresses, Neighbors, Area Ranges, Prefix SIDs IS-IS Instances, Interfaces, Settings, Levels, Segment Routing, Flex-Algos, Prefix-SIDs, SRv6 Locators EIGRP Routers, Address Families, Networks, Interfaces

Each entry opens a list of that kind of object. Most entries have an Add button and many have an Import button (see Importing).

docs.title: Objects and how they relate
docs.text:
Routing configuration is a tree. You build it from the top down, and each object points to its parent. The same shape repeats for every protocol:

Device ── protocol process (instance / router) ── area / address family / level ── interface
                                              └─ per-process extras (redistribution, ranges, ...)
Protocol Top Then Down to Static Static route (assigned to) Devices BGP Router (ASN, assigned to a device, site, region...) Scope (global or one VRF) → Address family → Peer address family Peers OSPF Instance (on a device, optionally in a VRF) Areas → Interfaces → Networks, Neighbors Redistribution, Virtual links, Summary addresses and Prefix SIDs hang from the instance; Area ranges from the area IS-IS Instance (on a device, optionally in a VRF) Levels, Segment routing, Flex-Algos, SRv6 locators Interfaces → Interface levels, Prefix-SIDs EIGRP Router (on a device) Address families Networks and Interfaces

The consequence: create the parent first. The Add form of an OSPF interface needs an OSPF instance and an OSPF area of that instance to exist already. If a form asks for something that does not exist, go back one level.

Use what NetBox already has. Devices, interfaces, IP addresses, prefixes, VRFs, ASNs, tenants and roles are standard NetBox objects. The plugin never copies them; it links to them. A prefix list entry points at a NetBox prefix, an OSPF network points at an IP address assigned to an interface, a BGP peer points at an IP address, a BGP router points at an ASN.

docs.title: What every object has
docs.text:
Because they are standard NetBox objects, all of them support:

  • Description, tags and custom fields, and a comments field on most.
  • Search, filters and export in the lists. The global NetBox search finds the plugin's objects.
  • Change log and journal entries, so you can see who changed a timer and when.
  • Cloning (the Clone button) which copies the fields that make sense to repeat.
  • Bulk edit and bulk delete from the lists.
  • The REST API and GraphQL for every model, under /api/plugins/routing/.

docs.title: On the device page
docs.text: The device page gets a Static Routes tab with the routes assigned to it (and a counter). OSPF instances, IS-IS instances, EIGRP routers and BGP routers each show their children in tabs on their own detail page, for example an OSPF instance has an Interfaces tab and an OSPF area lists its interfaces.

docs.title: Importing in bulk
docs.text: Entries with an Import button accept CSV, YAML or JSON through the usual NetBox import form. Columns refer to related objects by name (a device by its name, an interface by its name and device), the same way core NetBox imports do. Use Import on a list to see the exact columns the form accepts; it is the quickest way to load hundreds of interfaces or peers.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text: Forms refuse combinations the protocols do not allow, with a message that says why. Examples: an OSPF dead interval that is not larger than the hello interval, an IS-IS prefix SID with both an index and a label, a prefix list entry whose le is longer than the address family allows. Each protocol page lists the rules and their RFC.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text: Authentication keys and BGP passwords are stored in plain text in the NetBox database, like any other custom field. They are shown in the interface (a few OSPF keys can also show their MD5 digest), so give view permission on these objects only to people who may see the keys. Keys are not added to the global search index.

docs.title: BGP
docs.text:
Routing → BGP

BGP-4 (RFC 4271) is the protocol that carries routes between autonomous systems and, inside a network, between routers (iBGP). The plugin models a BGP configuration with the same layers a router has: the router (your AS), the scopes (global table or a VRF), the address families negotiated in each scope, and the peers, plus templates so you do not repeat yourself.

docs.title: How it is organized
docs.text:
BGP router (ASN, assigned to a device / site / region / cluster / VM)
 ├─ Settings (router-wide options)
 ├─ Templates available to its peers: session, peer, policy
 └─ Scope (global table, or one VRF)
     ├─ Settings
     ├─ Address family (IPv4 unicast, VPNv4, EVPN, ...)
     │   └─ Peer address family ── policy (prefix lists, route maps)
     └─ Peer (neighbor IP address)
         ├─ Settings
         └─ Peer address families

Build it in this order: ASN (NetBox IPAM) → Router → Scope → Address family → Peer → Peer address family. Templates can be created at any time and attached later.

docs.title: Routers
docs.text:
BGP → Routers

A router is "this AS, on this device (or site, region, cluster...)".

Field Meaning ASN A NetBox ASN (IPAM → ASNs). Four-octet ASNs are fine (RFC 6793). Name Optional label. Assigned to What the BGP process runs on: a device, virtual machine, site, location, region, site group, cluster or cluster group. Assign it to a site or region when the same BGP configuration applies to all the devices there. Tenant Optional owner. Session / Peer / Policy templates The templates peers of this router may use.

docs.title: Scopes
docs.text:
BGP → Scopes

A scope selects where the BGP configuration applies: the global routing table (no VRF) or a single VRF. Per-VRF BGP, as used by VPN services (RFC 4364), has one scope per VRF.

docs.title: Address families
docs.text:
BGP → Address Families

The kinds of routes the router exchanges in a scope. BGP carries more than IPv4 thanks to the multiprotocol extensions (RFC 4760); each address family is negotiated separately between the peers. The plugin offers:

Family Used for Standard IPv4 Unicast, IPv6 Unicast Normal internet and internal routing RFC 4271, RFC 4760 IPv4 / IPv6 Multicast Multicast routing information RFC 4760 VPNv4 / VPNv6 (Unicast and Multicast) L3VPN: customer routes with route distinguishers RFC 4364 (VPNv4), RFC 4659 (VPNv6) IPv4 / IPv6 / VPNv4 / VPNv6 Flowspec Distributing traffic filtering rules RFC 8955, RFC 8956 L2VPN VPLS Layer 2 VPN over BGP RFC 4761 L2VPN EVPN Ethernet VPN, data-center overlays RFC 7432 RTFILTER Route-target constrained distribution, to send VPN routes only where wanted RFC 4684 LINK-STATE Topology information for controllers RFC 7752 NSAP Legacy OSI addresses RFC 4760 (address family registry)

A scope can have each family once.

docs.title: Peers
docs.text:
BGP → Peers

A peer is one BGP neighbor.

Field Meaning Scope The router scope the session belongs to (global or a VRF). Peer The neighbor's IP address (a NetBox IP address). Source The local address to open the session from, usually a loopback. Remote AS The neighbor's ASN. Same as the router's ASN means iBGP, different means eBGP. Local AS Optional, a different ASN to present to this neighbor (used in AS migrations; a vendor feature). Enabled Administratively enable or disable the session. Status Active, Planned, Offline or Failed: the lifecycle of the session in your documentation (it is not read from the network). BFD profile Detect failure fast, see BFD. TTL The TTL of the session's packets. For directly connected eBGP set 255 and the expected hop count so the router drops spoofed packets: this is the Generalized TTL Security Mechanism, RFC 5082. Password The shared secret of the TCP session, stored as plain text. BGP session protection with a password is the TCP MD5 option, RFC 2385 (superseded in the standards by TCP-AO, RFC 5925). Peer template / Session template Inherit settings, see Templates. Tenant Optional owner.

docs.title: Peer address families
docs.text:
BGP → Peer Address Families

What a neighbor exchanges in each address family and under which policy: an address family of the scope (for example IPv4 unicast) plus the filters applied to that peer in that family.

Field Meaning Assigned to A peer or a peer template. Address family One of the scope's address families. Enabled Activate the family for the neighbor. Prefix list in / out Prefix lists (routing objects) that filter what is received from and sent to the neighbor. Route map in / out Route maps that filter or modify routes in each direction. Policy template Apply a policy template.

docs.title: Templates
docs.text: Templates remove repetition: define the shared part once and make peers point at it. There are three kinds because they inherit different things.

docs.title: Session templates
docs.text:
BGP → Session Templates: the properties of the TCP session. They can inherit from a parent session template, so you can build a base "all eBGP peers" template and refine it per customer type.

Fields: parent, enabled, local AS, remote AS, TTL, BFD profile, password, tenant.

docs.title: Policy templates
docs.text: BGP → Policy Templates: the filters (prefix lists in/out, route maps in/out). A policy template can have several parents; a peer address family points at one.

docs.title: Peer templates
docs.text:
BGP → Peer Templates: a group of neighbors that share a remote AS and per-address-family settings (the equivalent of a peer group). A peer points at one with Peer template.

Note. The plugin records which template each peer uses and what each template contains. It does not compute the final effective configuration of a peer; your configuration templates or automation combine them.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
BGP → Settings

Option-by-option settings that do not need their own field. A setting is a key and a value assigned to a router, a scope, an address family or a peer, so you can set an option at the level it applies to. Values are validated by type (yes/no, number or IP address).

Key Type Meaning Router ID IP address The BGP identifier, unique in the AS (RFC 6286). AS Dot Notation yes/no Write four-octet ASNs as high.low (RFC 5396). Graceful Restart yes/no Keep forwarding while the neighbor's BGP restarts (RFC 4724). Additional Paths (send / receive / install) number Advertise or accept more than one path per prefix (RFC 7911). Keep Alive, Hold Time seconds Session timers: the hold time is negotiated in the OPEN message and keepalives are sent about every third of it (RFC 4271). Default Metric number The metric (MED, RFC 4271) given to redistributed routes. Default Originate yes/no Advertise a default route to the neighbor (vendor feature). eBGP / iBGP / MP eBGP / MP iBGP Distance number Administrative distance of routes learned from each kind of session (vendor feature). Maximum Paths, Maximum Paths (secondary) number Equal-cost multipath: how many paths are installed (vendor feature). Auto summary yes/no Summarize routes at classful boundaries (legacy; disabled on modern platforms).

docs.title: EIGRP
docs.text:
Routing → EIGRP

EIGRP (Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol) is documented in RFC 7868 (informational: it was a Cisco protocol before it was published). The plugin models the configuration of an EIGRP process: which devices run it, in which address families, on which networks and interfaces.

docs.title: How it is organized
docs.text:
EIGRP router (device, mode) ─┬─ Address family (IPv4 / IPv6, optional VRF)
                             ├─ Network (a NetBox prefix, optional address family)
                             └─ Interface (a device interface, optional address family)

docs.title: Routers
docs.text:
EIGRP → Routers

One record per EIGRP process on a device.

Field Meaning Device The device that runs the process. Mode Classic Router (a numbered autonomous system process, the original configuration style) or Named Router (the newer named mode, where the process has a name and address families live inside it). Name The name, for named mode. Unique per device. Process ID The autonomous system number, for classic mode. Router ID Optional, the 32-bit identifier written like an IPv4 address; it has to be unique in the network.

docs.title: Address families
docs.text:
EIGRP → Address Families

The protocol runs one instance per address family. A family record belongs to a router and sets IPv4 or IPv6, an optional VRF (so the same router can run EIGRP in several VRFs) and an optional router ID that overrides the router's. A router cannot have the same family twice in the same VRF.

docs.title: Networks
docs.text:
EIGRP → Networks

The network statements: the NetBox prefix whose interfaces take part in EIGRP. Choose the router and, in named mode, the address family.

docs.title: Interfaces
docs.text:
EIGRP → Interfaces

Per-interface settings.

Field Meaning Interface A device interface. Passive The interface is advertised in EIGRP but sends no hellos and forms no neighbors; the usual setting for user-facing ports. BFD Use BFD (RFC 5880) for fast neighbor failure detection. Authentication Message Digest, Key Chain or Null (none). RFC 7868 defines the packet authentication. Passphrase The key, stored as plain text.

docs.title: Standards behind it
docs.text: Feature Standard The protocol, router ID, passive interfaces, authentication RFC 7868 BFD RFC 5880 Classic and named modes, VRF address families Cisco configuration styles; RFC 7868 describes the protocol, not the CLI

docs.title: IS-IS
docs.text:
Routing → IS-IS

IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System) is a link-state interior routing protocol like OSPF, popular in service-provider and data-center backbones. It was defined by ISO for OSI networks (ISO/IEC 10589) and adapted to carry IP in RFC 1195; IPv6 support is RFC 5308. The plugin models the instances that run on your devices, their levels and interfaces, authentication, and the modern segment-routing extensions.

docs.title: Concepts in two minutes
docs.text:
• Levels. IS-IS has two: Level 1 routes inside an area, Level 2 routes between areas (the backbone). A router can be Level-1, Level-2 only, or Level-1-2 (both).
  • NET (Network Entity Title). The address of the router in the form 49.0001.0000.0000.0001.00: an authority/format part, the area (49.0001), a 6-byte system ID (0000.0000.0001, unique per router) and a final 00.
  • Metric style. Narrow metrics are limited to 63 per link; wide metrics are 24 bits and are required for traffic engineering and segment routing (RFC 5305).

docs.title: How it is organized
docs.text:
IS-IS instance (a process on a device, optionally in a VRF)
 ├─ Level (Level-1 / Level-2 settings of the instance)
 ├─ Segment routing (SR-MPLS, SRv6, SRGB/SRLB)
 ├─ Flex-Algo        ├─ SRv6 locator        └─ Settings
 └─ Interface (device interface + address family)
     ├─ Interface level (per-level metric and hello settings)
     ├─ Prefix-SID
     └─ Settings

docs.title: Instances
docs.text:
IS-IS → Instances

Field Meaning Device, VRF Where the process runs. IS-IS can run once per VRF. Process tag The name of the process (router isis <tag>); empty for the unnamed process. Unique per device. NET The Network Entity Title, validated against the format above. Empty is allowed while you are drafting. IS type Level-1, Level-2 only or Level-1-2. Empty means the platform default (Level-1-2). Metric style Wide, Narrow or Transition (both, for migrating between the two). Empty means the platform default. Overload bit Set the overload bit: other routers stop using this router for transit traffic, while still reaching its own prefixes (ISO 10589). Used for maintenance. Overload on startup, timeout Set it for a number of seconds after boot so the router joins the network gradually. Suppress / ignore attached bit The attached bit tells Level-1 routers that this Level-1-2 router reaches other areas, so they use it as a default route. Suppress stops the router from setting it; ignore stops it from installing the default route toward routers that do (ISO 10589). Distance Administrative distance. Maximum paths Equal-cost paths installed (ECMP). Reference bandwidth Mbps used to derive default interface metrics. Traffic engineering Enable IS-IS TE extensions (RFC 5305).

docs.title: Timers
docs.text: Field Meaning SPF initial / maximum wait Delay before recomputing paths after a change, and the longest back-off (ms), see RFC 8405. LSP initial / maximum wait The same for generating a new LSP (ms). LSP lifetime, refresh interval, MTU How long a LSP lives, how often it is refreshed (seconds) and the size limit of a LSP (bytes).

docs.title: Fast reroute and micro-loops
docs.text: Field Meaning Standard Fast reroute Precompute a backup for every route: LFA, Remote LFA or TI-LFA. Turn on per interface with FRR below. RFC 5286, RFC 7490; TI-LFA is an IETF draft for segment routing Micro-loop avoidance Delay forwarding after a change to avoid short-lived loops while routers converge. RFC 8333

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
IS-IS has authentication in four places; each takes a type and a key, and one without the other is refused:

Where Protects Area password (instance) LSPs and SNPs of Level 1. Domain password (instance) LSPs and SNPs of Level 2. Level LSPs of that level, set on the Level object. Hello (interface) The hello PDUs of one interface, so only trusted routers become neighbors.

Types: Cleartext (the original ISO 10589 password, weak), MD5 (RFC 5304) and HMAC-SHA-1 / HMAC-SHA-256 (RFC 5310). Keys are stored as plain text.

docs.title: Levels
docs.text:
IS-IS → Levels

The settings of the instance for one level: one record per instance and level.

Field Meaning Level Level-1 or Level-2. Default metric Metric for interfaces in this level that have none. Wide metrics only Use only the wide metric TLVs in this level. Preference, labeled preference Route preference of this level, and of paths that use segment-routing labels. Disabled Switch the level off on this instance. Authentication type / key Level authentication, see above.

docs.title: Interfaces
docs.text:
IS-IS → Interfaces

A device interface that takes part in IS-IS, one record per address family: an interface that runs IPv4 and IPv6 has two. The interface must be on the instance's device.

Field Meaning Instance, Interface The process and the device interface. Address family IPv4 or IPv6. Circuit type The levels the interface takes part in: Level-1, Level-2 only or Level-1-2. Network type Point-to-point or Broadcast. On broadcast networks a DIS (designated intermediate system) is elected, like the OSPF DR; point-to-point links have no election and form adjacencies faster. Metric The cost of the link. Passive Advertise the interface's prefix but form no adjacency. Hello authentication See above. BFD Use BFD for fast failure detection (RFC 5882). FRR, FRR protection Include the interface in fast reroute (or exclude it), and whether to protect against link failure or node failure too. CSNP interval, retransmit interval, LSP interval Protocol pacing: how often the DIS sends the complete sequence number PDU (s), the LSP retransmission interval (s) and the pacing between LSPs (ms). Mesh group Limit LSP flooding on dense meshes, or blocked to stop flooding on the interface (RFC 2973).

docs.title: Interface levels
docs.text:
Open an interface and use its Levels tab (there is no menu entry for this object).

Settings that differ per level on one interface: metric, hello interval, hello multiplier (how many hellos can be missed), priority for the DIS election (higher wins) and passive.

docs.title: Segment routing
docs.text:
IS-IS → Segment Routing

Segment routing steers traffic with a list of labels or addresses carried in the packet, without per-flow state in the core. IS-IS advertises the segments: RFC 8667 for SR-MPLS. One record per instance.

Field Meaning Enabled SR-MPLS on this instance. SRv6 enabled SRv6 on this instance; the locators are separate objects (below). Prefix-SID range global or a named/explicit range. SRGB start / range The Segment Routing Global Block: the labels reserved for prefix SIDs, which should be the same on every router. Start and range go together. SRLB start / range The Segment Routing Local Block, for local SIDs such as adjacency SIDs. Also together. Maximum SID depth How many labels the router can push. Tunnel table preference Preference of SR tunnels against other tunnel types.

docs.title: Prefix-SIDs
docs.text:
IS-IS → Prefix-SIDs

The SID of an interface's prefix. Exactly one of SID index (an index into the SRGB) or SID label (an absolute label) is set, never both. Algorithm is 0 (SPF) or a Flex-Algo (128 to 255). Flags: Node SID (the prefix identifies a single node, a /32 or /128), No PHP (do not pop the label at the penultimate hop), Explicit null (use explicit null instead), Readvertise (the SID is leaked from another level or protocol). One SID per interface and algorithm.

docs.title: Flex-Algo
docs.text:
IS-IS → Flex-Algos

Flexible Algorithm lets the network compute its own constrained paths, for example "lowest delay, avoiding links of colour red" (RFC 9350).

Field Meaning Algorithm ID 128 to 255. Metric type igp-metric, delay-metric or te-metric. Priority Used when routers define the same algorithm differently; the highest priority wins. Admin groups: exclude / include any / include all The affinities (link colours) the paths must avoid or use. Comma-separated names.

docs.title: SRv6 locators
docs.text:
IS-IS → SRv6 Locators

With SRv6 the segments are IPv6 addresses (RFC 8986; IS-IS advertisement in RFC 9352). A locator is the IPv6 prefix of the router, split into block and node parts (LOC = Block:Node in RFC 8986).

Field Meaning Name, prefix The locator and its IPv6 prefix. Unique name per instance. Algorithm 0 (SPF) or a Flex-Algo (128 to 255). Anycast The locator is shared by several nodes. Micro-segment (uSID) A compressed-SID locator. Flavor The END behaviour flavours, for example psp usd. Block / node / function / argument length The sizes in bits of the parts (RFC 8986). The total cannot exceed 128. Empty derives them from the prefix. IS-IS level Advertise in one level only; empty means both. Enabled The instance advertises the locator. Vendor extensions JSON for vendor details with no cross-vendor equivalent.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
IS-IS → Settings

A key and value assigned to an instance or interface for the options that do not need their own field. The value must match the type of the key (yes/no, number or address).

Key Meaning SPF Second Wait, SPF Rapid Runs, LSP-Gen Second Wait Extra SPF and LSP generation back-off controls (vendor-specific). TE IPv4 / IPv6 Router-ID Stable address used in traffic-engineering advertisements (RFC 5305, RFC 6119). Graceful Restart Keep forwarding while IS-IS restarts (RFC 8706). LDP-IGP Sync Do not use a link for traffic until LDP is up (RFC 5443). Prefix Suppression Do not advertise transit-only link prefixes (RFC 6860). Multi-Topology Separate topologies per address family (RFC 5120). Log Adjacency Changes, Advertise Passive Only, Default Route Tag, IGP Shortcut, Hello Padding, RIB Priority Vendor features without an RFC.

docs.title: Standards behind IS-IS
docs.text: Standard What it gives the plugin ISO/IEC 10589 The protocol: levels, NET, overload and attached bits, cleartext authentication RFC 1195, RFC 5308 IS-IS for IPv4 and for IPv6 RFC 5304, RFC 5310 MD5 and HMAC-SHA authentication RFC 5305, RFC 6119 Wide metrics and traffic engineering (IPv4 / IPv6) RFC 5120 Multi-topology RFC 2973 Mesh groups RFC 5286, RFC 7490, RFC 8333 Fast reroute and micro-loop avoidance RFC 8405 SPF back-off RFC 8667, RFC 9350 Segment routing and Flex-Algo RFC 8986, RFC 9352 SRv6 RFC 8706, RFC 5443, RFC 6860, RFC 5882 Graceful restart, LDP sync, prefix suppression, BFD

docs.title: OSPF
docs.text:
Routing → OSPF

OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) is a link-state interior routing protocol: every router floods descriptions of its links, and each one computes the shortest paths on its own. The plugin models OSPF version 2 for IPv4, defined in RFC 2328, and the extensions that real networks use on top of it. Defaults and ranges follow the RFC, and each feature below says which RFC it comes from.

Scope. OSPFv3 (IPv6, RFC 5340) is not modelled yet. Networks, summary addresses and ranges accept IPv4 only, and the router ID is an IPv4-style identifier.

docs.title: How it is organized
docs.text:
OSPF instance (a process on a device, optionally in a VRF)
 ├─ Area ── Interface (a device interface in the area) ── Network (its IP addresses)
 │                                                    └─ Neighbor (static neighbors)
 │   └─ Area range
 ├─ Redistribution
 ├─ Summary address
 ├─ Virtual link
 └─ Prefix SID

Build it top-down: Instance → Area → Interface → Network. The rest are optional extras of the instance or area.

docs.title: Instances
docs.text:
OSPF → Instances

An instance is one OSPF process: "OSPF on this device, in this VRF".

docs.title: Identity
docs.text: Field Meaning Name The process name or number, as on the device. Device The device that runs it. VRF Optional. OSPF can run once per VRF. Router ID The 32-bit identifier of the router in the OSPF domain (RFC 2328 §C.1), written like an IPv4 address. It must be a valid IPv4 address, not 0.0.0.0 and without a mask, and it should be unique in the network. Instance ID Lets several OSPF processes run over the same link: routers form an adjacency only with a neighbor that has the same ID (RFC 6549). Default 0.

docs.title: Default route
docs.text: Field Meaning Default originate Advertise a default route (0.0.0.0/0) into OSPF. By default it is advertised only while the router has a default route itself. Always Advertise it even when no default route exists locally. Metric, metric type Metric of the originated route, and whether it is Type 1 (E1) or Type 2 (E2) (see redistribution). These options require Default originate.

docs.title: Timers
docs.text: Field Meaning Default SPF initial / short / long delay, time to learn, hold-down The SPF back-off algorithm: after a topology change the router waits a short time before recomputing paths, and backs off when changes keep coming, to protect the CPU during instability (RFC 8405). Milliseconds. The delays must be in order. 50 / 200 / 5000 ms, learn 500 ms, hold-down 10000 ms LSA minimum interval Minimum time between originations of the same LSA (MinLSInterval, RFC 2328). 5000 ms LSA minimum arrival Minimum time before accepting a new copy of the same LSA (MinLSArrival, RFC 2328). 1000 ms

docs.title: Stability and maintenance
docs.text: Field Meaning Max metric (router LSA) Advertise the maximum metric for the router's links so that transit traffic avoids the router while it is being maintained or started (RFC 6987). The on startup value keeps it for that many seconds after boot; it requires the max-metric option. Graceful restart Disabled, planned restarts only, or planned and unplanned restarts: the router keeps forwarding while OSPF restarts (RFC 3623). Restart period Seconds neighbors wait for the restart to finish: 1 to 1800, default 120. Helper, strict LSA checking Whether this router helps neighbors that restart gracefully, and whether it ends the help when the topology changes (RFC 3623; both enabled by default, as the RFC suggests).

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: Field Meaning Max LSAs, threshold, warning only Cap on the number of LSAs the process accepts, the percentage that triggers a warning (default 75) and whether to only warn at the limit. Protects the router from being flooded with routes. External LSDB limit, exit overflow interval Cap on non-default AS-external LSAs and how long to wait before leaving the overflow state; 0 means until restart. This is the database overflow feature of RFC 1765.

docs.title: Routing behaviour
docs.text:
Field Meaning RFC 1583 compatibility Rules used to choose among AS-external routes. RFC 2328 §16.4.1 changed them; the default (enabled) keeps the old behaviour so mixed networks agree. All routers in an OSPF domain should use the same setting. Reference bandwidth Mbps that gets an interface cost of 1, used to derive the cost of interfaces that have none. Raise it on networks with links faster than 100 Mbps. Maximum paths Equal-cost paths installed (ECMP), 1 to 64. Distances Administrative distance of intra-area, inter-area and external routes (1 to 255). Default metric Metric given to redistributed routes that have none. Passive interface default Interfaces are passive (no neighbors) unless configured otherwise. BFD on all interfaces Enable BFD on every OSPF interface. Log adjacency changes (+ detail) Log neighbor state changes, or every state change.

Empty optional fields mean "use the platform default".

docs.title: Advanced features
docs.text:
Field Meaning Standard Opaque capability Support opaque LSAs, the extensible LSA type that carries traffic-engineering and segment-routing data. Required by the two features below. RFC 5250 TE router address Stable address of the router in traffic-engineering LSAs, usually a loopback. Empty uses the router ID. RFC 3630 Segment routing, SRGB start/size Advertise segment routing and the label block (SRGB) the router uses. Requires opaque LSAs. RFC 8665, RFC 7684 LDP sync, hold-down Advertise the maximum metric on interfaces until LDP is up on them, so traffic never takes a path without labels. RFC 5443

The instance's authentication is described in Authentication.

docs.title: Areas
docs.text:
OSPF → Areas

OSPF divides a large network into areas; routers in an area know the detail of that area only, and area border routers (ABRs) summarize it to the rest. Area 0 (the backbone) connects all the others.

Field Meaning Instance The OSPF instance. Area ID A number (10) or dotted form (0.0.0.10). Unique within the instance. Area type See the table below. Type What it means Standard Standard A normal area: receives all routes. RFC 2328 Backbone Area 0. Area 0 must be of type Backbone, and no other area can be. RFC 2328 Stub No external (AS-external) routes inside; the ABR injects a default route instead, which shrinks the routing table of small routers. RFC 2328 §3.6 Totally Stubby A stub area that also blocks inter-area routes: only a default route enters. Vendor extension of the stub area NSSA A stub-like area that can still contain an ASBR (a router that imports external routes). Its external routes travel as type 7 LSAs and the ABR translates them to type 5. RFC 3101 Totally NSSA An NSSA that also blocks inter-area routes. Vendor extension of RFC 3101

Area 0 cannot be a stub area, and an area cannot be removed while it has interfaces.

Extra settings for Stub and NSSA areas:

Field Meaning Default cost Cost of the default route the ABR advertises into the area (stub and NSSA only). Translate always (NSSA) Always translate type 7 into type 5 LSAs (RFC 3101). No redistribution (NSSA) Do not import redistributed routes into the NSSA. Default originate (NSSA) Originate a default type 7 LSA into the NSSA.

For all areas:

Field Meaning Standard Traffic engineering Originate TE LSAs (opaque type 10) for the area. Needs opaque LSAs on the instance, and cannot be switched off while interfaces use TE attributes. RFC 3630 Fast reroute Compute loop-free alternate next hops for the routes of the area; each interface picks its mode. Cannot be switched off while interfaces use it. RFC 5286

docs.title: Interfaces
docs.text:
OSPF → Interfaces

An OSPF interface says "this device interface takes part in OSPF, in this area, with these settings". An interface can run one OSPF instance. The interface must be on the same device and VRF as the instance, and the area must belong to the instance.

docs.title: Basics
docs.text: Field Meaning Interface A device interface (NetBox DCIM). Instance, Area Where it takes part. Network type See below. Passive Advertise the interface's network but form no neighbors on it. Priority Designated Router election priority, 0 to 255 (default 1). 0 means the router never becomes DR. Cost Output cost, 1 to 65535. Empty derives it from the interface bandwidth and the instance's reference bandwidth. BFD Use BFD for fast neighbor failure detection. MTU ignore Skip the MTU mismatch check when forming adjacencies. The MTU itself comes from the device interface.

docs.title: Network types
docs.text:
The network type tells OSPF how the link behaves (RFC 2328):

Type Meaning Broadcast A LAN such as Ethernet: neighbors are discovered with multicast and a DR is elected. The default. Point to Point A link between two routers; no election. Non Broadcast (NBMA) A multi-access network without broadcast (such as Frame Relay): neighbors are configured by hand and a DR is elected. Point to Multipoint One interface connected to several routers treated as a set of point-to-point links. Point to Multipoint Non Broadcast The same, with neighbors configured by hand. Loopback A loopback interface, advertised as a host route.

docs.title: Timers
docs.text:
Field Meaning Default Hello interval Seconds between Hello packets. 10 Dead interval Seconds without Hellos before a neighbor is declared down. It must be larger than the hello interval. 40 Retransmit interval Seconds between LSA retransmissions. 5 Transmit delay Estimated seconds to transmit an LSA. 1

The defaults are the values of RFC 2328 appendix C.3 for a LAN. Routers must agree on hello and dead intervals to become neighbors.

docs.title: Other interface options
docs.text: Field Meaning Standard TTL security, hops Send OSPF packets with TTL 255 and drop received ones whose TTL shows they crossed more than the allowed hops, so only directly connected routers can speak OSPF. Use 1 hop for direct neighbors. RFC 5082 Prefix suppression Do not advertise the interface's prefixes in the router LSA, hiding transit-only networks. RFC 6860 Flood reduction Flood LSAs as DoNotAge to cut refresh traffic in stable networks. RFC 4136 Demand circuit Suppress periodic Hellos and refreshes on a link that is charged by use. RFC 1793 Database filter all out Do not flood any LSA out of the interface. Vendor feature TE metric, max reservable bandwidth, admin group Traffic-engineering attributes of the link: its TE metric, bandwidth that can be reserved, and the colour mask used by affinity rules. They require traffic engineering on the area. RFC 3630 Adjacency SID Local MPLS label for the adjacency over this link (16 to 1048575). Needs segment routing on the instance. RFC 8665 Fast reroute Protect the traffic with a precomputed alternate: Loop-Free Alternate or Remote LFA. Needs fast reroute on the area. RFC 5286, RFC 7490 LDP sync Override the instance's LDP synchronization for this interface; leave empty to inherit. RFC 5443

docs.title: Networks
docs.text:
OSPF → Networks

The IP addresses of an OSPF interface that OSPF advertises: pick the interface and a NetBox IP address assigned to that interface. An interface may have several networks, each only once. An interface with no addresses (an unnumbered interface) has no networks. Only IPv4 is accepted, and the network is derived from the address and its mask. Deleting the IP address in IPAM removes the network.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
OSPFv2 can authenticate its packets so that only trusted routers join the domain (RFC 2328 appendix D). The same block of fields appears on instances, areas, interfaces and virtual links:

Type Meaning Null No authentication. Simple Password A clear-text password, up to 8 characters. Weak: only protects against mistakes. Message Digest A cryptographic digest with a key ID (0 to 255) and a key of up to 16 characters for MD5. Key Chain The name of a key chain configured on the device, which rotates keys. No key is stored here.

For message digest, choose the algorithm: MD5 (RFC 2328), or HMAC-SHA-1/256/384/512 (RFC 5709). The key is stored as plain text; tick Show MD5 to also display the MD5 digest the key produces on devices that store it that way.

docs.title: Inheritance
docs.text:
Authentication is set where convenient and inherited downwards: an interface uses its own authentication; if it has none it uses its area's; if the area has none it uses the instance's. So you can set one authentication on the instance, override it for an area, and override it again on a single interface.

The plugin checks that the pieces agree: an interface cannot go without authentication, or use a different type, in an area that requires one; an area's authentication is checked against its interfaces; and the instance default is checked against the interfaces of the areas that use it. The three types (null, simple, cryptographic) cannot be mixed within an area, because routers need the same type to talk. Virtual links must agree with the backbone's type.

docs.title: Redistribution
docs.text:
OSPF → Redistribution

Redistribution imports routes learned some other way into OSPF as external routes, turning the router into an ASBR.

Field Meaning Protocol Connected, Static, EIGRP, BGP, OSPF or IS-IS. Source The process to take routes from, for EIGRP, BGP, OSPF and IS-IS. It must be on the same device as the instance. Connected and static have no source. Metric Metric of the redistributed routes. Metric type E1 or E2. With E2 (the default) the metric stays the same across the OSPF domain; with E1 the internal cost to reach the ASBR is added, which makes routers prefer the closer ASBR (RFC 2328 §16.4.1). Subnets Redistribute subnets, not only classful networks. On by default. Route tag A tag set on the routes, to filter them later (RFC 2328 external route tag). Route policy Name of a route policy/route map applied to the routes. OSPF route types When the source is OSPF, which kinds of routes to redistribute.

Rules: each protocol (and each source) can be redistributed once per instance; an OSPF instance cannot be redistributed into itself; a BGP source must be a router of the same device.

docs.title: Virtual links
docs.text:
OSPF → Virtual Links

Every area must touch the backbone. When one cannot, a virtual link (RFC 2328 §15) tunnels the backbone through a transit area to the remote ABR.

Field Meaning Transit area The area the link crosses. It must be a standard area of the same instance, and cannot be deleted while a link crosses it. Remote router ID Router ID of the ABR at the other end. One link per transit area and remote router. Timers, TTL security, authentication The same as an interface. Authentication falls back to the backbone's, then the instance's, and its type must agree with the backbone's.

docs.title: Summary addresses
docs.text:
OSPF → Summary Addresses

Summarization of the external routes an ASBR redistributes: one LSA for the prefix replaces many. It reduces the size of the routing table and of the database.

Field Meaning Prefix IPv4 prefix without host bits set (10.0.0.0/8, not 10.0.0.1/8). One summary per prefix per instance. Not advertise Suppress the routes covered by the prefix instead of summarizing them. Route tag Tag set on the summary route.

docs.title: Area ranges
docs.text:
OSPF → Area Ranges

An area range is summarization at an area border router (RFC 2328 appendix C.2): the ABR advertises one summary for all the area's routes inside the range to the other areas.

Field Meaning Area The area whose routes are summarized. Prefix IPv4 range without host bits. One per area. Range type Summary of intra-area routes, or on an NSSA NSSA external: the addresses of the type 7 LSAs translated into type 5 (RFC 3101 §3.2). NSSA external ranges only exist on NSSA areas; the same prefix can be both a summary and an NSSA range. Advertise Advertise the range as one route, or DoNotAdvertise to hide the routes of the range.

docs.title: Neighbors
docs.text:
OSPF → Neighbors

On non-broadcast (NBMA) and point-to-multipoint networks routers cannot find each other with multicast Hellos, so the neighbors are configured by hand (RFC 2328 appendices C.5 and C.6). A neighbor is identified by its IP address on the network.

Field Meaning OSPF interface The interface the neighbor is reached through. Its network type must be Non Broadcast or one of the Point to Multipoint types; other types have no configured neighbors. IP address The neighbor's interface address: a unicast IPv4 address on a network of the interface, and not the interface's own. One entry per address per interface. Priority Eligibility of the neighbor to become DR, 0 to 255 (0 = not eligible). Required on non-broadcast networks, where a DR is elected; not used on point-to-multipoint ones. Poll interval Seconds between Hellos while the neighbor is down, much larger than the hello interval. Non-broadcast only.

docs.title: Prefix SIDs
docs.text:
OSPF → Prefix SIDs

With segment routing the router advertises a Segment Identifier for each prefix, and traffic is steered by stacks of labels (RFC 8665, using the extended prefix LSA of RFC 7684). It needs segment routing and opaque LSAs on the instance.

Field Meaning Prefix The IPv4 prefix the SID is for (no host bits). SID type Index into the SRGB (the label is the block's start plus the index) or Absolute label (a local MPLS label, 16 to 1048575). An index must fit the SRGB. Algorithm SPF (0) or Strict SPF (1). Node SID The prefix identifies the router itself (N flag, RFC 7684). It must be a host prefix (/32). No PHP The penultimate hop must not remove the label (NP flag, RFC 8665). Explicit null Upstream neighbors replace the SID with an explicit null label (E flag, RFC 8665).

One SID per prefix and algorithm. You cannot disable segment routing while SIDs exist, nor shrink the SRGB below an existing index.

docs.title: What happens when you delete things
docs.text: Delete Result An OSPF instance Refused while it has interfaces. Its unused areas, redistributions, virtual links, summary addresses and Prefix SIDs go with it. An area Refused while it has interfaces; its ranges go with it. An OSPF interface Its networks and neighbors go with it. A device Its OSPF interfaces go with it. An IP address in IPAM The OSPF network that used it is removed.

docs.title: Standards behind OSPF
docs.text: RFC What it gives the plugin RFC 2328 The protocol: router ID, areas, interface types and timers, authentication, virtual links, ranges, external route types RFC 3101 NSSA areas RFC 3623 Graceful restart RFC 3630 Traffic engineering extensions RFC 4136, RFC 1793 Flood reduction, demand circuits RFC 5082 TTL security RFC 5250 Opaque LSAs RFC 5286, RFC 7490 Loop-free alternates, remote LFA RFC 5443 LDP/IGP synchronization RFC 5709 HMAC-SHA authentication RFC 6549 Multi-instance OSPFv2 RFC 6860 Hiding transit-only networks RFC 6987 Max-metric router LSA RFC 7684, RFC 8665 Extended prefix/link LSAs and segment routing RFC 8405 SPF back-off RFC 1765 Database overflow

docs.title: Static routes
docs.text:
Routing → Static → Static Routes

A static route is a route you configure by hand instead of learning it from a routing protocol. It is the simplest object in the plugin: one record describes the route, and you assign it to the devices that carry it.

Standards. Static routes are not a protocol, so there is no RFC behind them. The plugin only checks what a route needs to be meaningful: a destination and a way to reach it.

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
Field Meaning Name Optional label ("default via ISP A"). Prefix The destination, IPv4 or IPv6 with its mask (0.0.0.0/0, 2001:db8::/32). VRF Optional. Leave empty for the global routing table. Next hop The IP address to forward to. Interface next hop The outgoing interface name, for routes without an IP next hop (a point-to-point link, for example). Metric The route's preference when several routes to the same prefix exist; lower wins. Defaults to 1. Permanent Marks a route that stays installed even if its next hop becomes unreachable (the permanent keyword on some platforms). Tag Optional number to match the route in policies, for example when redistributing static routes into OSPF. Devices The devices that have this route configured.

A route needs a next hop: either an IP next hop, an interface next hop, or both. The form refuses a route with neither.

docs.title: Typical uses
docs.text:
• A default route on many devices. Create the route once and select all the devices it applies to, instead of one record per device.
  • Floating static routes. Create the backup route with a higher Metric than the primary.
  • Route in a VRF. Select the VRF; the same prefix can then exist in several VRFs.
  • Seeing a device's routes. Open the device and use the Static Routes tab, which shows the routes assigned to it and how many there are.

docs.title: Where static routes connect to other protocols
docs.text: OSPF can redistribute static routes (OSPF redistribution); the Tag is the usual way to pick which ones.
